action.new:
Reading the :attr:`port` attribute will raise a :exc:`ValueError` if
   an invalid port is specified in the URL.  See section
   :ref:`urlparse-result-object` for more information on the result object.

   Port validation is deferred: constructing the result with :func:`urlparse`
   or :func:`urlsplit` never raises for a bad port.  The :exc:`ValueError`
   is raised only when the :attr:`port` attribute is read.  The port
   component is valid when it consists of one or more ASCII decimal digits
   whose integer value lies in the range 0 through 65535 inclusive.  An
   absent port or an empty port component (a colon with no digits following)
   yields :const:`None`.  Any other form---a minus sign, a non-digit
   character, a non-ASCII digit, or an out-of-range integer---causes
   :exc:`ValueError`.

   .. doctest::
      :options: +NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE

      >>> from urllib.parse import urlparse
      >>> # Construction always succeeds, even with an invalid port:
      >>> r = urlparse("http://example.com:70000/")
      >>> r.netloc
      'example.com:70000'
      >>> # Accessing .port raises:
      >>> try:
      ...     r.port
      ... except ValueError as e:
      ...     print(e)
      Port out of range 0-65535
      >>> # Accepted boundary values:
      >>> urlparse("http://example.com:0/").port
      0
      >>> urlparse("http://example.com:65535/").port
      65535
      >>> # Absent or empty port yields None:
      >>> urlparse("http://example.com/").port is None
      True
      >>> urlparse("http://example.com:/").port is None
      True
      >>> # Non-numeric port:
      >>> try:
      ...     urlparse("http://example.com:abc/").port
      ... except ValueError as e:
      ...     print(e)
      Port could not be cast to integer value as 'abc'

   Unmatched square brackets in the :attr:`netloc` attribute will raise a
   :exc:`ValueError`.
